stem: A bag contains 3 red marbles, 5 blue marbles, and 2 green marbles. If one marble is selected at random, what is the probability that it is blue?
explanation: The total number of marbles is \(3 + 5 + 2 = 10\). The number of blue marbles is 5, so the probability of selecting a blue marble is \(\dfrac{5}{10} = \dfrac{1}{2}\). Option A (\(\dfrac{1}{5}\)) results from dividing 2 by 10 or an arithmetic error in simplification. Option B (\(\dfrac{3}{10}\)) uses the count of red marbles instead of blue. Option D (\(\dfrac{3}{5}\)) incorrectly counts 6 blue marbles or misreads the problem.

stem: A standard deck of 52 playing cards contains 4 suits of 13 cards each. Two cards are drawn at random without replacement. Given that the first card drawn is a heart, what is the probability that the second card drawn is also a heart?
explanation: After one heart is drawn, 12 hearts remain out of 51 total cards, so the conditional probability is \(\dfrac{12}{51}\). Option A (\(\dfrac{13}{52}\)) ignores that a heart was already removed, treating the draws as independent. Option B (\(\dfrac{12}{52}\)) correctly reduces the hearts to 12 but fails to reduce the total from 52 to 51. Option D (\(\dfrac{13}{51}\)) reduces the total deck but does not remove the drawn heart from the heart count.

stem: In a class of 30 students, 18 play soccer, 12 play basketball, and 6 play both soccer and basketball. If a student is selected at random from those who play soccer, what is the probability that the student also plays basketball?
explanation: This is a conditional probability question: P(basketball | soccer) = (number who play both) / (number who play soccer) = \(\dfrac{6}{18} = \dfrac{1}{3}\). Option A (\(\dfrac{1}{5}\)) divides 6 by 30 (the entire class), computing P(both) rather than the conditional probability. Option C (\(\dfrac{2}{5}\)) divides 12 by 30, computing P(basketball) unconditionally. Option D (\(\dfrac{1}{2}\)) divides 6 by 12, conditioning on basketball players instead of soccer players.

skill: Inference from Sample Statistics and Margin of Error
stem: A random sample of 200 voters in a city found that 120 support a new park proposal. Based on this sample, what is the best estimate of the proportion of all voters in the city who support the proposal?
explanation: The sample proportion is \(\dfrac{120}{200} = 0.60\), which is the best estimate of the population proportion. Option A (0.40) computes the proportion who do NOT support the proposal (80/200). Option B (0.50) assumes an even split without using the data. Option D (0.80) results from an arithmetic error such as dividing 120 by 150 or misreading the sample size.

skill: Inference from Sample Statistics and Margin of Error
stem: A survey of 400 randomly selected residents found that 52% prefer candidate A, with a margin of error of 4 percentage points. Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?

options.text: Exactly 52% of all residents prefer candidate A.
Between 48% and 56% of all residents are likely to prefer candidate A.
Candidate A will win the election with certainty.
At least 56% of all residents prefer candidate A.

explanation: A margin of error of 4 percentage points means the confidence interval for the true population proportion is \(52\% \pm 4\%\), or from 48% to 56%. Option A incorrectly treats the sample statistic as the exact population parameter. Option C overstates the conclusion; since the interval includes values below 50%, certainty is not warranted. Option D uses only the upper bound and ignores the lower bound of the interval.

skill: Inference from Sample Statistics and Margin of Error
stem: Two independent random samples are taken from the same population. Sample 1 has 100 respondents and finds a mean of 74 with a margin of error of 6. Sample 2 has 400 respondents and finds a mean of 71 with a margin of error of 3. Which of the following statements is best supported?

options.text: Sample 1 provides a more precise estimate because its sample mean is higher.
Sample 2 provides a more precise estimate because its margin of error is smaller.
Both samples are equally precise because they come from the same population.
Neither sample is reliable because their means differ by 3.

explanation: Precision of an estimate is determined by the margin of error, not the magnitude of the sample statistic. Sample 2 has a margin of error of 3, which is smaller than Sample 1's margin of error of 6, so Sample 2 provides the more precise estimate. This is consistent with the larger sample size reducing variability. Option A confuses a higher sample mean with greater precision; these are unrelated concepts. Option C ignores that sample size affects precision even when sampling from the same population. Option D incorrectly claims both are unreliable; differing sample means are expected due to sampling variability and do not indicate unreliability.

skill: Evaluating Statistical Claims: Observational Studies and Experiments
stem: Researchers found that students who eat breakfast daily have higher test scores than students who skip breakfast. The study recorded students' existing habits without any intervention. What type of study is this?

options.text: A controlled experiment
An observational study
A census
A sample survey

explanation: Because the researchers observed students' existing habits without assigning treatments or interventions, this is an observational study. Option A is incorrect because a controlled experiment requires the researchers to assign subjects to treatment and control groups. Option C is incorrect because a census collects data from every member of a population, which is not described here. Option D is incorrect because a sample survey collects self-reported data via questionnaire, whereas this study recorded habits and test scores as observed data.

skill: Evaluating Statistical Claims: Observational Studies and Experiments
stem: A company randomly assigns 500 employees to either a standing-desk group or a traditional-desk group and measures productivity after 3 months. The standing-desk group shows a 12% increase in productivity. Which conclusion is most appropriate?

options.text: Standing desks are associated with higher productivity, but a causal relationship cannot be established.
Standing desks cause a 12% increase in productivity for all workers.
There is evidence that standing desks cause increased productivity among the employees in this study.
The results are invalid because the employees knew which group they were in.

explanation: Because participants were randomly assigned to treatment groups, this is a randomized experiment, which does support a causal conclusion for the study population. Option A incorrectly applies the limitation of observational studies; random assignment allows causal inference. Option B overgeneralizes to all workers, whereas the conclusion applies to the employees in this company. Option D is incorrect because awareness of group assignment does not automatically invalidate results in a randomized experiment; while blinding strengthens an experiment, the random assignment still supports causal inference.

skill: Evaluating Statistical Claims: Observational Studies and Experiments
stem: A health researcher surveys 1,000 adults selected at random from a city and finds that those who exercise regularly report lower stress levels than those who do not. The researcher concludes that exercise reduces stress. Which of the following is a valid criticism of this conclusion?

options.text: The sample size of 1,000 is too small to draw any conclusion.
Because participants were not randomly assigned to exercise or not exercise, confounding variables may explain the difference.
The random selection of participants ensures that a causal conclusion is valid.
The study should have used a smaller sample to reduce variability in the results.

explanation: This is an observational study because participants self-selected into exercise or no-exercise groups; no treatment was assigned. Without random assignment, confounding variables (such as income, free time, or general health) could explain the observed association, so a causal conclusion is not warranted. Option A is incorrect because 1,000 is a reasonably large sample for drawing statistical conclusions. Option C confuses random selection (which supports generalizability to the population) with random assignment (which supports causal inference); random selection alone does not justify a causal claim. Option D is incorrect because reducing sample size increases variability and weakens conclusions.
